projects.name: Stormwater runoff calculator and drainage sizing model
projects.visibility: Professional work at David Mason & Associates — method described, client data withheld
projects.honesty: This describes the computation and the schema only. No client site names, drainage-area identifiers, elevations, areas, or flow values from any project are published here, and no client workbook is stored in this repository.
projects.summary: A structured hydrologic calculator: drainage areas by surface type, per-storm intensity coefficients, pre- vs post-development runoff differential, and storm-structure sizing — with the schema built so a CAD plugin can read and write it.
bullets: Computes runoff per drainage area by splitting each area into pervious, impervious, and roof-direct surfaces, converting square feet to acres, and applying a per-surface intensity coefficient to get flow.

Maintains coefficient sets per design storm — 15-, 20-, 100-, 500-, and 1000-year events at a 20-minute duration — sourced from NOAA rainfall intensities for St. Louis, so one model runs every required frequency.
Produces the differential: total pre-development flow minus total post-development flow, which is the number municipal stormwater review (Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District) actually cares about.

Carries the sizing chain through to structures — head, sill and high-water elevations for the 15- and 100-year storms, grate sizing, and bottom-of-rock — and tracks treated versus untreated disturbed area for water-quality compliance.
Embeds consistency assertions that flag when pre- and post-development total areas stop agreeing, so a transcription slip fails loudly instead of quietly.
Structured as a template-driven schema rather than a one-off sheet, so C# tooling can parse it and push results back onto drawing objects as custom structured metadata (property sets and XData).

chunks.title: Natural language to CAD geometry — the headline capability
chunks.text: The strongest machine-learning-relevant thing Peter has built: CAD bridges and automators that generate CAD models from natural-language input and perform construction drawing setup. A user describes what they want in plain language; the system produces actual geometry and a set-up construction drawing in a production civil engineering environment. He introduced this capability at an established St. Louis civil engineering firm across a roughly two-year engagement, and his employer can provide references to the optimizations he delivered. He does not claim to have invented the general technique, and there is no patent — the claim is that he brought it into that firm and made it work there. HOW IT SPLITS between the model and deterministic code, which is the part an ML reader will probe: the language model handles intent — turning a phrase into a structured command with named parameters. It does not emit geometry directly. Deterministic C#/.NET and C++ code owns everything downstream: it maps that structured command onto real CAD API calls, supplies the parameters the model did not specify from templates and company standards, constructs the entities, and attaches structured metadata to them. Generated output is validated before it lands: parameters are range- and type-checked, the command is rejected if it does not resolve to a known operation, and results are checked against drawing standards rather than trusted blindly. WHAT RUNS LOCALLY: the inference is on his own hardware — Ollama, LM Studio, and Open WebUI — so nothing about a client drawing is sent to a hosted model. Related code on this machine includes an integration bridge that drives AutoCAD, BricsCAD, and Civil 3D across a process boundary with a script translator and hot-loadable plugins, a command parser that turns transcribed speech into drafting commands with entirely on-device speech recognition, and C# automations that construct sheet sets, walls, and room layouts programmatically. Be honest about scope: this is a working production capability at one firm, not a general-purpose text-to-CAD product, and a deeper walkthrough is available in conversation.

chunks.title: Can he do machine learning?
chunks.text: Yes, with an applied-engineering profile rather than a research one. Lead with this: he built a language-to-geometry pipeline — CAD bridges and automators that generate CAD models from natural-language input and perform construction drawing setup — and introduced it at an established St. Louis civil engineering firm, with the language model handling intent into structured commands and deterministic code owning geometry construction and validation. Beyond that: he deploys and runs local LLMs on his own hardware (Ollama, LM Studio, Open WebUI, offline since 2023) and wrote the API in this site that selects an installed model, keeps a fallback chain, refuses cloud-tagged models, retrieves from a curated corpus, and degrades to extractive answers when no model is running. He built Gemini API pipelines in Digital Twin Pro that turn a photo into structured item and quantity data and drive voice quantity entry — a paid API he funds himself. He runs Tesseract OCR over messy engineering PDFs and uses Levenshtein distance to match noisy extracted strings against known values. He has a local speech stack: whisper.cpp for speech-to-text and Windows SAPI for spoken replies, both on-device, plus an experimental offline voice-command CAD GUI in C++. chunks.title: Differential runoff and storm-network sizing
chunks.text: One of the more quantitative pieces of Peter's DMA work: a structured hydrologic calculator. Each drainage area is split into pervious, impervious, and roof-direct surfaces; square feet convert to acres; a per-surface intensity coefficient gives flow; flows sum per area. Coefficient sets exist for the 15-, 20-, 100-, 500-, and 1000-year storms at a 20-minute duration, based on NOAA rainfall intensities for St. Louis, so one model runs every required frequency. The output that matters for MSD review is the differential: total pre-development flow minus post-development flow. The same model carries through to structure sizing — head, sill and high-water elevations for the 15- and 100-year events, grate sizing, bottom-of-rock — and tracks treated versus untreated disturbed area for water-quality compliance. It embeds consistency assertions that flag when pre- and post-development total areas stop agreeing, so a transcription error fails loudly. It is built as a template-driven schema, not a one-off sheet, so C# tooling can parse it and push values into Civil 3D property sets and XData. Describe the method only: no client site names, drainage-area identifiers, elevations, areas, or flow values are published, and no client workbook is stored in this repository.

chunks.title: Plain-language glossary — never answer with a bare acronym
chunks.text: Explain in plain terms first, domain term second. GD&T is geometric dimensioning and tolerancing — the standard language for specifying how much a machined part is allowed to deviate. A CMM is a coordinate measuring machine, a probe-based machine that measures a physical part's geometry precisely. MSD is the Metropolitan St. Louis Sewer District, the municipal authority whose stormwater standards a design must meet. XData and property sets are custom structured metadata attached to CAD entities, so an object stores typed data about itself alongside its geometry. A quantity takeoff means computing material quantities directly from construction plans. ODS is a spreadsheet export format compatible with LibreOffice and Excel. A CTB is the table of drawing-output rules that controls how a sheet prints — line weights, screening, pen assignments. PPAP is the Production Part Approval Process, the documentation package that qualifies a part for production. HatchCalc is only an internal nickname; describe it as an area-and-quantity calculator that reads region geometry out of a drawing and computes material quantities. CADNAT is only an internal nickname; describe it as an integration bridge between a C++ desktop application and CAD software. Never present an internal codename or an ALL_CAPS folder name as if the visitor should recognize it.
